verses.text: In those days was Hezekiah sick and near death. Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, came to him, and said to him, “Yahweh says, ‘Set your house in order, for you will die, and not live.’”
Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to Yahweh,
and said, “Remember now, Yahweh, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Isaiah, saying,
“Go, and tell Hezekiah, ‘Yahweh says, the God of David your father, “I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.
I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will defend this city.
This shall be the sign to you from Yahweh, that Yahweh will do this thing that he has spoken.

Behold, I will cause the shadow on the sundial, which has gone down on the sundial of Ahaz with the sun, to return backward ten steps. So the sun returned ten steps on the sundial on which it had gone down.”’”
The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick, and had recovered of his sickness.
I said, “In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol.  I am deprived of the residue of my years.”
I said, “I won’t see Yah, Yah in the land of the living. I will see man no more with the inhabitants of the world.

My dwelling is removed, and is carried away from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up, like a weaver, my life. He will cut me off from the loom. From day even to night you will make an end of me.
I waited patiently until morning. He breaks all my bones like a lion. From day even to night you will make an end of me.
I chattered like a swallow or a crane. I moaned like a dove. My eyes weaken looking upward. Lord, I am oppressed. Be my security.”
What will I say? He has both spoken to me, and himself has done it. I will walk carefully all my years because of the anguish of my soul.
Lord, men live by these things; and my spirit finds life in all of them: you restore me, and cause me to live.
Behold, for peace I had great anguish, but you have in love for my soul delivered it from the pit of corruption; for you have cast all my sins behind your back.
For Sheol  can’t praise you. Death can’t celebrate you. Those who go down into the pit can’t hope for your truth.
The living, the living, he shall praise you, as I do today. The father shall make known your truth to the children.
Yahweh will save me. Therefore we will sing my songs with stringed instruments all the days of our life in Yahweh’s house.
Now Isaiah had said, “Let them take a cake of figs, and lay it for a poultice on the boil, and he shall recover.”
Hezekiah also had said, “What is the sign that I will go up to Yahweh’s house?”

footnotes.content: Isaiah walks into the dying king's room with a hard word: settle your affairs, your time is ending. This is the mercy of warning—Hezekiah has one last chance to turn his face to the Lord. When Jesus said "blessed are those who mourn," He knew that sickness can strip away pretense and leave a man alone with what matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king turns his face to the wall—not away in despair, but inward, toward silence, toward Yahweh. This simple gesture shows us where real strength lives. Not in the throne or the crown, but in the broken heart that knows whom to seek.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah's plea is honest: I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart. His tears are not self-pity but grief that his time may end. He does not ask for more years; he asks that the God who knows his heart will remember him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord hears. Not after a long wait, not through an angel—His word comes directly to the prophet. Prayer in the dark is met with immediate word. The silence we fear often hides the Lord who is already turning to answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifteen more years. The Lord sees the tears, hears the prayer. This is grace that heals not because we deserve it but because the Father delights in rescuing those who call to Him. And He adds the city's salvation too—Hezekiah's faithfulness becomes a doorway for the Lord's protection over all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not only Hezekiah's life is prolonged, but Jerusalem itself will be shielded from Assyrian conquest. His prayer matters beyond his own breath. When we pray in faith, we stand in a current of mercy that flows far beyond ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will give a sign. In mercy, He offers proof—not to test our faith but to hold it steady through what comes next. Faith does not shrink from signs; it welcomes them as love letters from the hand of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shadow on Ahaz's sundial returns ten steps backward. Time, which seemed to move only forward toward death, bends at the word of the Lord. This is not magic but a sign written in the heavens themselves—the God who made time is not bound by it. In the promise of resurrection, we glimpse that He is reversing death itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now we enter Hezekiah's own words, his writing after sickness and recovery. What follows is a king's testimony, raw and real. He does not smooth it over or make himself look noble—he simply tells what he felt and what he learned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I go into the gates of Sheol in the middle of my years. Hezekiah has tasted the nearness of death, been robbed of his remaining time. This is the language of true mourning—not pretty, but piercing. When we face our own end, we learn what Hezekiah knew: all the throne in the world is nothing without breath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I won't see Yah anymore. The greatest loss is not life itself but the breaking of communion with the living God. To be cut off from His presence is the truest death. When Hezekiah names this loss, he names what every human heart fears most—to be separated from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My dwelling is removed like a shepherd's tent taken down. I have rolled up my life like a weaver's work cut from the loom. The images pile up—unmoored, finished, ended. In his terror, Hezekiah speaks the language of unraveling. But the very act of naming it aloud is the beginning of naming it to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I waited patiently until morning. He breaks my bones like a lion. Hezekiah endures the night of suffering, waiting for dawn that may never come. The Lord is present even in this—not to explain the pain, but to receive the man who cries out. Patience in anguish is not resignation; it is faith that leans toward Him even in darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I chattered like a swallow, moaned like a dove. My eyes weaken looking upward. In his weakness, Hezekiah's sounds are those of birds—small, fragile, lifted toward heaven. "Lord, I am oppressed. Be my security." There is no strength left but petition. And that is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What will I say? He has spoken to me, and done it. I will walk carefully all my years because of the anguish of my soul. Hezekiah has glimpsed the seriousness of his life. Recovery does not return him to carelessness—it deepens him. He will hold his years gently, gratefully, carefully, marked by the grace that returned him from the gate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lord, men live by these things, and my spirit finds life in all of them. He speaks of the Lord's restoration and the life that flows from it. Not doctrine, but testimony: to be restored by Yahweh's hand is to taste what life itself is meant to be. Everything—breath, thought, the turning of days—becomes a gift held in that restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For peace I had great anguish. But you have cast all my sins behind your back. The Lord transforms the meaning of Hezekiah's suffering: it led him not to despair but to reconciliation, to the removal of his guilt. He learns that mercy is not cheap—it costs the Lord's own faithfulness to cast sin aside. And still He does it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheol can't praise you. Death can't celebrate you. This is the stirring truth beneath Hezekiah's whole testimony: only the living praise the Lord. Death is not the end; it is the severing of worship. To be alive is to have a voice. To sing is to have still a chance to glorify the God who gave you breath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The living, the living, he shall praise you. Readers today hear an echo in these words—we too have been snatched from the gates of death, spared by mercies we did not earn. Like Hezekiah, we are meant to tell the next generation what we have learned: that the Lord's truth is worth passing on, and every breath is a chance to testify.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh will save me. Therefore we will sing my songs with stringed instruments all the days of our life in Yahweh's house. This is the covenant of recovery: once you have been healed, your song becomes the witness. Hezekiah's gladness is not private—it is music meant to resound in the house of the Lord, drawing others to see His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let them take a cake of figs and lay it on the boil. Isaiah's word is practical—the Lord uses remedy as well as miracle. The fig poultice is real medicine; the healing that follows is real grace. Both together show us that the Lord cares for the whole of us, body and soul, using the world He made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What is the sign that I will go up to Yahweh's house? Even recovered, Hezekiah longs for confirmation—for one more word that holds him steady. The Lord answers in time, proving that He is not stingy with assurance to those whose hearts are turned toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
